candidate.answerReason: Among 28 equally likely pairs of physical bills, 12 contain exactly one twenty, 1 contains two twenties, and 1 contains two tens. Hence 14/28=1/2 qualify.

methods.label: Count pairs of physical bills
methods.explanation:
Distinguish the physical bills, even when their values agree. There are \(8\cdot7\) equally likely ordered draws, because the first bill is not replaced. Each unordered pair occurs in two orders, so there are
\[
\frac{8\cdot7}{2}=28
\]
equally likely pairs.

Any pair containing a twenty has a sum above \(\$20\). Without a twenty, only the pair of two tens reaches \(\$20\), since every other available pair totals at most \(\$15\).

For exactly one twenty, choose one of the \(2\) twenties and one of the \(6\) other bills, giving \(2\cdot6=12\) pairs. There is also one pair containing both twenties and one pair containing both tens. These disjoint cases include every qualifying pair, so the probability is
\[
\frac{12+1+1}{28}=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
choice D.
methods.levelReason: The pair count is derived directly from ordered draws, and the favorable cases use elementary addition and multiplication.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task targets probability for equally likely selections of physical bills. The method recognizes unordered pairs, derives their count from the two possible draw orders, and counts disjoint denomination cases. Sampling without replacement explains the seven choices on the second draw. No factorial formula, conditional-probability formula, or distribution model is needed.
